titre: Archaeoraptor: The 1999 “Missing Link” Was a Composite
accroche: In 1999, National Geographic presents a Chinese fossil as the link between dinosaurs and birds. A scanner and Xu Xing show a composite.
contenu_vulgarise:
In February 1999, at the Tucson mineral show in Arizona, the Utah museum The Dinosaur Museum, run by Stephen and Sylvia Czerkas, buys a fossil from Liaoning, in northeastern China. The specimen mixes bird and dinosaur traits: the body of a primitive bird, the tail of a dinosaur. It seems to be everything people are looking for: the link between the two groups. On October 15, 1999, a press conference announces it. In November 1999, National Geographic devotes an article to it under the title “Feathers for T. rex?”, signed by Christopher Sloan, the magazine's art editor. The text was not peer-reviewed.

## A Story That Does Not Hold Together

The fossil comes from the shale quarries of Xiasanjiazi, where farmers dig illegally and sell their finds to dealers. According to National Geographic's account as repeated by Wikipedia, one of them glued several pieces together. Warning signs abound. On March 6, 1999, the paleontologist Philip Currie notices that the two feet are symmetrical, mirror images of each other. On July 29, 1999, the paleontologist Timothy Rowe runs the specimen through an X-ray scanner at the University of Texas at Austin: the tail and the lower legs are not part of the main fossil. In August 1999, Nature rejects the manuscript, then Science rejects it too. National Geographic publishes anyway.

## The Missing Piece

It is the Chinese paleontologist Xu Xing who settles it. In October 1999, he notices that the tail resembles that of a small, still unnamed dinosaur. He goes to Liaoning and finds there a fossil whose tail matches that of the specimen so exactly that it can only be its counterslab, with two identical yellow oxide spots. On December 20, 1999, he writes to the authors and to Sloan: the fossil is a fake. National Geographic publishes the results of its investigation in October 2000. Rowe and his colleagues describe the forgery in Nature in 2001: bones of a primitive bird and of a dromaeosaurid dinosaur had been assembled.

## At Least Two Real Animals in a Fake

The tail belongs to Microraptor zhaoianus, a small winged dinosaur named in December 2000. The upper body belongs to Yanornis, a bird, identified in 2002. The legs come, according to Wikipedia, from a still unknown animal. The fossil returned to China in June 2000.

What was fake is not what people think. The fragments came from real fossils: each belonged to a real animal, and the two identified animals are scientific discoveries in their own right. The fake was the animal itself, composed of pieces that had never lived together. A question remains that this fossil already raised: how many pieces bought at a market, with no known place of discovery, are on display without anyone having scanned them?

repere.texte: Presented in 1999 as the link between dinosaurs and birds, Archaeoraptor is a composite: bones of a primitive bird and of a dromaeosaurid dinosaur, demonstrated by X-ray scanner (Rowe et al., Nature, March 29, 2001).
repere.source: Rowe et al., “Forensic palaeontology: The Archaeoraptor forgery,” Nature, vol. 410, 2001, pp. 539-540

carte.punch: The 1999 “missing link” mixed at least two animals.
carte.idee: Presented by National Geographic in 1999, Archaeoraptor combined the tail of a dinosaur and the body of a bird. An X-ray scanner, then the twin tail found by Xu Xing, demonstrated it. The fragments were real, the animal fake.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Page on the dinosaur whose tail was mounted on Archaeoraptor.

quiz.question: What made it possible to demonstrate that Archaeoraptor was a composite?
choix: An X-ray scanner and an identical tail found on another Liaoning fossil
A radiometric dating giving a different age for each bone of the specimen
An ancient DNA analysis showing several species in the bone fragments
The testimony of the Czerkases, who supposedly recognized the assembly at the time of purchase
quiz.explication: Rowe's scan showed that the tail and the lower legs did not belong to the main fossil, and Xu Xing found in Liaoning the exact counterslab of the tail. No dating of individual bones or DNA analysis figures in this demonstration, and the Czerkases at first disputed the assembly.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where and when was the Archaeoraptor fossil bought?
choix: From a Chinese museum in Liaoning, in March 1999
At the Tucson mineral show in Arizona, in February 1999
At an auction in Beijing, in January 1999
Directly at the Xiasanjiazi dig site, in April 1999
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The fossil was bought in February 1999 at the Tucson mineral show by the Dinosaur Museum in Utah, run by Stephen and Sylvia Czerkas.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who signed the National Geographic article presenting Archaeoraptor, and in what capacity?
choix: Philip Currie, who had noticed the symmetry of the feet
Timothy Rowe, who had scanned the fossil in Texas
Christopher Sloan, the magazine's art editor
Xu Xing, the paleontologist who uncovered the fraud
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The November 1999 article, signed by Christopher Sloan, National Geographic's art editor, had not been peer-reviewed.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Once the composite was exposed, to which animals were Archaeoraptor's fragments attributed?
choix: The tail to Microraptor zhaoianus and the upper body to the bird Yanornis
The whole skeleton to a single already known dromaeosaurid
The tail to a juvenile Tyrannosaurus and the body to a pterosaur
All the fragments to plaster casts with no fossil origin
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The tail belongs to Microraptor zhaoianus, named in December 2000, and the upper body to the bird Yanornis, identified in 2002.
